data.title: Gonorrhoea / urethral discharge — viva
data.summary: Sexually transmitted infections · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Gonorrhoea / urethral discharge** (Sexually transmitted infections)_

**Q1. What is gonorrhoea and its organism?**
- STI caused by Neisseria gonorrhoeae — Gram-negative intracellular kidney/bean-shaped diplococci; infects columnar/transitional epithelium (urethra, endocervix, rectum, pharynx, conjunctiva)

**Q2. Why does gonorrhoea not cause vaginitis in adult women?**
- Adult vagina has stratified squamous epithelium (oestrogen) resistant to gonococci; prepubertal girls (thin columnar-like epithelium) get vulvovaginitis

**Q3. Clinical features in men?**
- Incubation 2–5 days; profuse purulent urethral discharge, dysuria, meatal oedema; complications: epididymitis, prostatitis, periurethral abscess, Tysonian/Littre gland abscess, urethral stricture

**Q4. Gonococcal vs non-gonococcal urethritis?**
- Gonococcal: short incubation, profuse purulent discharge, Gram-negative intracellular diplococci
- NGU: longer incubation (1–3 weeks), scanty mucoid discharge, pus cells ≥2/oil immersion field without diplococci — Chlamydia trachomatis (D–K), Mycoplasma genitalium, Ureaplasma, Trichomonas

**Q5. What is disseminated gonococcal infection?**
- Arthritis–dermatitis syndrome: fever, migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis and few acral haemorrhagic pustules on erythematous base; or purulent monoarthritis; risk with menstruation, pregnancy, late complement (C5–C9) deficiency, SLE

**Q6. Investigations?**
- Gram stain of urethral smear (sensitivity >95% in symptomatic men; poor in women), culture on Thayer–Martin/modified New York City medium (antibiotic sensitivity), NAAT/PCR (most sensitive, multiple sites incl. pharynx and rectum)
- Screen for chlamydia, syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B/C

**Q7. Treatment?**
- CDC 2020/2021: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose (1 g if ≥150 kg); add doxycycline 100 mg twice daily × 7 days if chlamydia not excluded
- NACO syndromic: grey kit (kit 1) — cefixime 400 mg + azithromycin 1 g single dose for urethral discharge/cervicitis
- Treat partners; abstain for 7 days; test of cure for pharyngeal infection

**Q8. Why high-dose ceftriaxone?**
- Rising MICs and ceftriaxone-resistant strains; pharyngeal infection needs higher levels; azithromycin resistance makes dual therapy less reliable

**Q9. Ophthalmia neonatorum — prevention and treatment?**
- Prophylaxis at birth: 0.5% erythromycin or 1% tetracycline eye ointment (silver nitrate 1% — Credé method, historical)
- Treatment: ceftriaxone 25–50 mg/kg IM single dose (max 125 mg) and saline irrigation

## Quick spotter facts
- Profuse purulent urethral discharge with Gram-negative intracellular diplococci — gonococcal urethritis

_Sources: DYP Survival Guide for PG Dermatology Exam (Long case — Gonorrhoea); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e ch.132; NACO; CDC 2021. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
